title: Sorting fundamentals and common sorting algorithms
learningObjectives: Explain sorting as arranging elements under a defined ordering relation.
Trace bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort on a small sequence.
Compare the algorithms' typical time costs, extra space and stability characteristics.
Explain why insertion sort can perform well on small or nearly sorted inputs despite quadratic worst-case growth.
Use qsort with a comparator that returns negative, zero or positive without overflowing subtraction.
Test sorting with empty, one-element, duplicate, already sorted and reverse-sorted data.

understand.concept: Sorting rearranges elements so they follow a chosen order, such as ascending numeric order. Different algorithms make different trade-offs in comparisons, movement, extra memory, stability and performance on particular input patterns.
understand.whyItMatters: Sorted data supports easier reporting, grouping and binary search. Understanding the algorithm's properties helps select a suitable approach and avoid incorrect comparator logic.
understand.analogy: Sorting a hand of cards by repeatedly inserting each new card into the correct place resembles insertion sort. Selecting the smallest remaining card resembles selection sort.
understand.analogyLimit: Algorithm names alone do not guarantee a runtime. Performance depends on input size and pattern, implementation details, compiler and machine; stability and worst-case guarantees must be checked for the chosen algorithm.

explain.narrative:
A sorting algorithm must use a consistent ordering. For integers, ascending order means each preceding element is no greater than the next. Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps out-of-order pairs; a simple version is stable but usually performs quadratic work. Selection sort repeatedly selects the minimum remaining element and swaps it into place; it uses little extra memory but is generally not stable. Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by shifting larger elements right; it is stable when equal elements are not moved past one another and can be efficient on nearly sorted, small inputs, though its worst-case work is quadratic.

The C standard library provides qsort. Its comparator receives pointers to two elements and must return a negative, zero or positive value according to their ordering. Do not return a - b for arbitrary int values because signed subtraction can overflow. Instead compare with relational operators and return (a > b) - (a < b). qsort does not promise stable ordering among equal elements.

Validate the element count and size arguments, supply the correct element size and test duplicates, empty and one-element arrays, sorted input and reverse-sorted input. Measure performance for realistic data rather than assuming one algorithm is always best.

examples.title: Insertion sort for a small integer array
examples.explanation: At the start of each outer iteration, the prefix before i is sorted. The current item is inserted into that prefix by shifting only larger elements. The strict greater-than comparison leaves equal elements in their original relative order, making this implementation stable.

examples.title: A safe qsort comparator for int
examples.explanation: The comparator returns a negative value, zero or a positive value without subtracting arbitrary signed integers. The size and element count are derived from the array. qsort may reorder equal elements because it is not specified to be stable.

practise.guidedTask: Trace insertion sort on [6, 3, 5, 2]. After each outer pass, write the sorted prefix and the number of shifts performed.
practise.independentTask: Implement insertion sort and compare it with qsort for empty, single-element, duplicate, already sorted and reverse-sorted arrays. Explain stability, worst-case growth and why comparator subtraction can overflow.
hints: Define the ordering before selecting an algorithm.
Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix as it processes the array.
Stability means equal-key elements retain their relative order.
Selection sort and insertion sort both use little auxiliary storage in their basic array forms.
qsort's comparator must be consistent and must not overflow.
Test duplicates and reverse-sorted data, not only a convenient sample.

questions.prompt: What does a stable sorting algorithm guarantee?
options: Equal-key elements keep their original relative order
The algorithm always runs in O(n)
The array never changes
The algorithm uses no comparisons
questions.answer: Equal-key elements keep their original relative order
questions.explanation: Stability concerns the relative order of elements whose keys compare equal.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm builds a sorted prefix by inserting each next item into its correct position?
options: Insertion sort
Selection sort
Binary search
Linear search
questions.explanation: Insertion sort shifts larger prefix elements and places the next item in the gap.

questions.prompt: Why is returning a - b unsafe in a qsort comparator for arbitrary int values?
options: The subtraction can overflow signed int
It always returns zero
qsort requires floating-point results
Subtraction sorts the array twice
questions.answer: The subtraction can overflow signed int
questions.explanation: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour; relational comparisons avoid that subtraction.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the C qsort function is correct?
options: Its comparator returns a negative, zero or positive result and qsort is not guaranteed stable
It always preserves the order of equal elements
It sorts only integers
Its comparator must return exactly -1 or 1
questions.answer: Its comparator returns a negative, zero or positive result and qsort is not guaranteed stable
questions.explanation: The comparator contract permits any negative, zero or positive result; stability is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Which input pattern can be favourable for insertion sort?
options: A small or nearly sorted sequence
Every reverse-sorted sequence is guaranteed linear
A sequence too large to fit in memory
An unsorted linked list with no random access
questions.answer: A small or nearly sorted sequence
questions.explanation: Insertion sort often performs few shifts when the input is already or nearly sorted.
